facts.claim: GIA: there are two main processes used to create laboratory-grown diamonds, High-Pressure High-Temperature (HPHT) and Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD). (Apify web-fetch, full page read.)

GIA: HPHT mimics some key conditions of natural diamond formation; a capsule containing a carbon source and a mixture of metals is heated to about 1300 to 1600°C under pressures of 5 to 6 GPa (equivalent to 150 to 190 km beneath the Earth's surface). An HPHT press can also be used to treat diamond colour.

GIA: CVD is dramatically different from natural growth; it occurs at near-vacuum pressure, a microwave-activated plasma releases carbon that rains onto diamond seeds and crystallises layer by layer at about 700 to 1200°C. Final size depends on seed size and growth time.

GIA: treatments can be used to enhance laboratory-grown diamonds, and GIA's lab-grown report states whether there is evidence of post-growth treatment; GIA can determine whether a stone was grown by HPHT or CVD using spectroscopy and other testing.
facts.conflicts: 4Cs page describes the older 'Laboratory-Grown Diamond Report'. GIA's current service page (fact_10) mentions growth type and post-growth treatment only for the lab-grown COLOURED diamond reports; whether the colourless Quality Assessment states treatment is not confirmed. Writer: say 'GIA can identify growth method and post-growth treatment', not what every document states.

facts.claim: GIA: laboratory-grown diamonds have the same crystal structure as natural diamonds (tightly bonded carbon atoms), resulting in nearly the same chemical, optical and physical properties. By eye the difference can potentially be indistinguishable; they are separated by very different growth histories, which experienced labs like GIA detect with advanced instrumentation.

GIA: simulants (commonly glass, moissanite and cubic zirconia) are not diamonds; they are completely unrelated to diamond at the atomic level and are easily identifiable by their optical and physical characteristics. GIA says buying a simulant can be a great option as long as it is an informed decision.

GIA: natural and lab-grown diamonds are separated by the types, distributions and concentrations of atomic-level defects and impurities; screening equipment and advanced gemological and spectroscopic testing at labs like GIA allow the two to be confidently separated. GIA's iD100 desktop instrument helps jewellers distinguish natural from lab-grown diamonds, simulants and some treated diamonds.

GIA history: first CVD diamonds 1952 (Union Carbide), HPHT soon after (General Electric) for industrial use; first gem-quality lab-grown diamonds by GE researchers in the 1970s; colourless lab-grown diamonds available in commercial quantities from the mid-2010s.

GIA press release, 2 June 2025: GIA would start using descriptive terms for the quality of laboratory-grown diamonds and no longer use the colour and clarity nomenclature it developed for natural diamonds; the report confirms the item is laboratory-grown and places it in 'premium' or 'standard'; stones below the minimum get no GIA designation. GIA's Tom Moses: more than 95% of lab-grown diamonds entering the market fall into a very narrow range of colour and clarity. Existing GIA lab-grown reports remain valid.

GIA press release, 26 August 2025: the GIA Laboratory-Grown Diamond Quality Assessment launched 1 October 2025 (previous D-to-Z lab-grown services available until 30 September 2025). Stones are described as 'Premium' or 'Standard' based on an overall assessment of clarity, colour and cut; stones not meeting the 'Standard' minimum receive no GIA assessment. Each stone's girdle is laser inscribed 'Laboratory-Grown' plus the GIA quality assessment number. Minimum size 0.15 ct. (Fee figures on the page deliberately excluded.)

GIA service page (current, read 29 Oct 2026): Laboratory-Grown Diamond Quality Assessment is an 'overall quality evaluation that classifies each laboratory-grown diamond as Premium or Standard' for loose colourless to near-colourless lab-grown diamonds of 0.15 ct or more, with the girdle inscribed 'Laboratory-Grown' and the quality assessment number. Lab-grown COLOURED diamonds get separate reports that include growth type and post-growth treatment.
facts.conflicts: GIA's 4Cs consumer page (fact_04/fact_05 source) still describes a 'Laboratory-Grown Diamond Report' with 'detailed color and clarity specifications'. The service page and press releases are newer and govern; the 4Cs page appears outdated. Sister guide fact_21 is superseded on report naming.

facts.claim: GIA's 2025 rationale: describing lab-grown quality with descriptive terms is appropriate because most fall into a very narrow colour and clarity range, and the change is meant to help consumers understand the important differences in the two products' origin.

IGI: lab-grown diamonds IGI reports on carry an 'LG' prefix laser-inscribed on the girdle ahead of the report number, noted in the report comments; reports can be verified on igi.org by report number or QR code. (Carried from sister fact_22, WebSearch summary 2026-10-28; Apify fetch of igi.org on 2026-10-29 returned HTTP 202 with no content.)
facts.conflicts: Not read in full on either day. Writer may state 'IGI inscribes an LG prefix'; whether IGI still uses D-to-Z colour and clarity grades on lab-grown reports is not confirmed.

facts.claim: FTC Jewelry Guides 16 CFR 23.12(a): a diamond is a mineral consisting essentially of pure carbon crystallised in the isometric system; its hardness is 10, specific gravity about 3.52, refractive index 2.42. 23.12(c)(3): 'cultured' may describe laboratory-created diamonds with essentially the same optical, physical and chemical properties as mined diamonds only if qualified by a clear and conspicuous disclosure such as 'laboratory-created', 'laboratory-grown' or '[manufacturer name]-created' conveying it is not a mined stone. (eCFR current text, Apify fetch.)

FTC Jewelry Guides 16 CFR 23.25(b)-(c): it is unfair or deceptive to use 'gem', 'stone' or a precious stone name for a laboratory-grown, laboratory-created, [manufacturer name]-created, synthetic, imitation or simulated stone unless immediately preceded with equal conspicuousness by 'laboratory-grown', 'laboratory-created', '[manufacturer name]-created' (or like meaning) or 'imitation'/'simulated'; 'faux' is not an adequate disclosure; and 'laboratory-grown' etc. may only be used for a product with essentially the same optical, physical and chemical properties as the stone named.
facts.conflicts: Diamond-specific naming sits in 23.12; the 'immediately preceded with equal conspicuousness' wording is in 23.25(b), which FTC staff applied to diamonds in the 2019 letters (fact_17).

facts.claim: FTC: the Jewelry Guides were updated in July 2018 and give marketers guidance on non-deceptive claims for mined, laboratory-created and simulated diamonds.

FTC Business Blog, 2 April 2019: FTC staff sent warning letters to eight companies over lab-created and simulated diamond marketing; points included disclosing lab or simulant origin close to the word 'diamond' and product images (including social media, hashtags and URLs), avoiding confusing proprietary terms, keeping descriptors consistent (concern that 'cultured' could imply mined), and not hiding disclosures in FAQs or links.

FTC Business Blog, 2 April 2019: some companies described products as 'eco-friendly', 'eco-conscious' or 'sustainable'; marketers must have a reasonable basis for any environmental claim, and under the FTC Green Guides should steer clear of general environmental benefit claims because they are unlikely to substantiate all reasonable interpretations.

ACCC: any claim a business makes about its products must be accurate, truthful and based on reasonable grounds, whether or not it intends to mislead; this applies to advertising, websites, social media and anything staff say. The ACCC can require businesses to back up claims.

ACCC: premium claims, including 'green' or environmental claims, must be true, accurate and based on reasonable grounds and should be specific, as broad vague terms may mislead. In some circumstances silence (failing to disclose relevant information) can be misleading. Claims about the future need reasonable grounds at the time they are made.

No ACCC guidance, determination or enforcement action specific to lab-grown diamond disclosure was found on accc.gov.au or in search (29 Oct 2026). Trade press (Jeweller magazine) reports a ruling that a business must not use 'diamond' in isolation for lab-created jewellery without a clear and prominent qualifier, but the regulator is not named in the search summary.
facts.conflicts: Article not read in full; do not cite it as an ACCC action. Writer may say: no lab-grown-specific ACCC guidance was found; the general ACL rules apply.

facts.claim: GIA: lab-grown diamonds are offered 'at a reduced price point', and demand has risen in recent years. (Only general relative-cost statement sourced; no figures.)

Diamond is 10 on the Mohs scale (scratch resistance) but is not the toughest gem and can be cleaved or fractured by a hard blow. (Carried from sister fact_18; FTC 23.12(a) independently confirms hardness 10 for any diamond, fact_14.)
GIA Report Check lets you look up GIA results with the report number; the GIA App can also look up GIA reports.

Kimberley Process Certification Scheme (from 2003) covers rough diamonds and aims to exclude conflict diamonds from legitimate trade. (Carried from sister fact_32; for a link to the diamond buying guide only.)

insider_details.detail: Since 1 October 2025, a GIA document for a colourless lab-grown diamond reads 'Premium' or 'Standard', not a D-to-Z colour and clarity grade, so a couple comparing a GIA lab-grown stone with one graded elsewhere on the natural-style scales is not comparing like with like; ask which lab and which document type before comparing.

Older GIA lab-grown reports issued before October 2025 remain valid, so a ring bought from existing stock may still carry the earlier format; check the number on GIA's own Report Check rather than relying on the paper.

For a proposal planned abroad, carry the report and receipt: the girdle inscription ('Laboratory-Grown' plus number for GIA, an LG prefix for IGI) is what lets a jeweller at home or overseas match stone to paperwork, as lab-grown and natural can look identical by eye.

If a jeweller calls a stone 'eco-friendly' or 'sustainable', ask for the evidence in writing; both the FTC and the ACCC expect specific, substantiated environmental claims, and vague ones can mislead.
Hardness 10 applies to lab-grown and natural alike, but neither is unbreakable; for an active wearer, the setting protects the stone more than the choice of origin.
